judgments.catchwords: 1. At the heart of the present application lies a familiar tension in the conduct of litigation: on the one hand, a person who is reluctant to give evidence and, on the other, a party who considers that person's evidence necessary for the just determination of the dispute. The law recognises that a witness cannot always be left to decide for himself whether he will attend Court and give evidence. It therefore provides a mechanism by which his attendance may, where the requisite conditions are satisfied, be compelled. That mechanism is the subpoena process. 2. The present application concerns the limits of that process. The 5th Defendant, who is herself a party to these proceedings, seeks in Enclosure 233 to set aside a subpoena issued by the Plaintiff requiring her to attend Court to give evidence and to produce certain documents. The Plaintiff, on the other hand, maintains that the 5th Defendant is a material witness whose evidence should be available to the Court at trial. 3. The trial of the action has been fixed for March 2027. 4. The application is supported by the 5th Defendant's written submissions in Enclosure 239 and reply submissions in Enclosure 243. The Plaintiff's written submissions in opposition are contained in Enclosure 241, with the Plaintiff's reply submissions in Enclosure 245. 5. This Court has considered the Notice of Application, the affidavits filed by the parties, the pleadings and Issues to be Tried, the written submissions and reply submissions of the parties, and the authorities contained in the respective bundles.

judgments.catchwords: Offence under section 39B(1)(a) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 read together with section 34 of the Penal Code - Whether the trial judge should have informed at the close of the prosecution's case, that the defence was being called upon to answer a case of actual trafficking or presumed trafficking? - Overwhelming evidence proved the elements of custody, control, and knowledge - Actual possession of the impugned drugs was established - Section 180 (1) and (4) of the Criminal Procedure Code - Procedure after conclusion of case for prosecution - No statutory or legal requirement to state the presumption when calling for the defence - Formal verbal label for an evidentiary rule at the close of the prosecution's case is unnecessary - Statutory presumption of trafficking under section 37(da)(xvi) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 - Section 422 of the Criminal Procedure Code - Not vitiate the conviction - No miscarriage of justice - Failure either to make or to record such a finding does not ipso facto - The law does not require a mini-judgment or detailed legal reasons at the close of the prosecution’s case
